Europe has to take action to curb soaring oil and gas prices to prevent people from turning to populists and extremists, a senior EU official has said.

European Commissioner for Energy Dan Jørgensen Photograph: Omar Havana/ReutersDan Jørgensen, the European commissioner for energy and housing policy, said EU governments could choose actions to make fossil fuels cheaper as long as they were “targeted” and “temporary” so as not to derail the continent from its goal to tackle the climate crisis by drastically cutting carbon emissions.

Earlier this week European gas prices hit their highest level since the winter of 2022, when consumers faced rising prices in the wake of supply disruption following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Meanwhile global oil prices have surged to $92 a barrel, an increase of $20 a barrel since March with even bigger price increases in some product markets, the International Energy Agency reported this week

Speaking to the Guardian and other European newspapers, Jørgensen said the EU was approaching a “tough” winter for citizens and business with “no signs that the situation in the Middle East is improving”.

A Circle-K petrol station in downtown of Riga, Latvia. Photograph: Wojtek Radwański/AFP/Getty ImagesSince the US and Israel launched the war on Iran that unleashed spiralling oil and gas prices, the EU had spent an extra €110bn (£93bn) paying for energy it would not have spent if supplies had remained stable, according to EU estimates.

Faced with that situation governments and the EU had to take action to help people heat their homes and put petrol in their cars, the commissioner said, even if that meant favouring fossil fuels in the short-term.

Jørgensen, a former Danish climate and energy minister, pointed out that even in an average year nearly 50m people in Europe struggle to heat their homes.

“If we do not tackle what people see as their most fundamental problems every day… if they do not have the ability to pay their bills at the end of the month, there’s a risk that they will listen to populists and extremists.”

He said governments could subsidise fossil fuels if necessary, “but it needs to be targeted and it needs to be temporary.”

He was speaking on Wednesday when the European Commission proposed a one-year delay to the EU’s methane ⁠emissions rules for oil and gas imports under pressure from the US, but also France. The rules, due to ⁠take effect on January ⁠1, 2027, would have required foreign oil and gas suppliers to the EU to monitor and report methane, a super-polluting greenhouse gas.

Earlier this year the European Commission proposed a major overhaul of the EU’s emissions trading system, the EU’s flagship policy to cut polluting emissions. Green groups fear the plans will weaken what they see as the EU’s most effective tool in fighting planet-heating gases.

But many member states are looking for more, including scrapping an extension of the ETS to housing and transport.

EU leaders, who discussed fuel prices on Thursday, are expected to call for the EU executive “to examine and put forward as needed further measures to address soaring energy prices in the short term” according to a draft of their summit conclusions.

Europe has to take action to curb soaring oil and gas prices to prevent people from turning to populists and extremists, a senior EU official has said (16:03).

If EU citizens don’t see their “fundamental problems” addressed, they may turn “to populists and extremists,” Dan Jørgensen said.

EU leaders are meeting in Brussels to discuss energy prices, EU budget, Middle East, and Ukraine during a two-day summit attended by Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy (11:16, 11:57, 13:25, 15:08).

The meeting comes amid heightened tensions between Ukraine and the US, with EU leaders joining Kyiv in criticising the US-Russia diesel deal (10:36) and reported Starlink disruptions (9:45, 9:49).

We will pick up on tonight’s developments in tomorrow morning’s blog.

1h ago15.53 BSTNato's Rutte says he discussed 'importance of implementing energy ceasefire' with ZelenskyyAfter meeting with Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Nato’s Mark Rutte has said the pair discussed “the importance of implementing an energy ceasefire,” as well as “continuous support for Ukraine” from Nato allies.

1h ago15.33 BSTSerbian ruler’s secret role in ‘illegal’ effort to help Trump businessTom Burgisin Belgrade

Meanwhile, Serbia’s authoritarian ruler personally intervened to advance an allegedly illegal scheme to hand over a protected site in Belgrade for a Trump tower, the Guardian can reveal.

View image in fullscreenJared Kushner visiting Serbian president Aleksandar Vucic. Photograph: Instagram/Aleksandar VucicAleksandar Vučić summoned officials to a meeting at his presidential offices about the project, which has culminated in a landmark indictment of senior figures from his regime on charges of abuse of public office.

The criminal case is believed to be the first resulting from the Trumps’ global moneymaking campaign, described by critics as a “pay to play” arrangement where everything from sanctions relief to cutting-edge chips is available to those who enrich the first family and their associates.

The alleged scheme to override the protected status of a historic building in the Serbian capital looms over an election scheduled for 25 October, when Vučić will seek to extend his 12 years in power in the face of a mass protest movement spurred by government corruption.

View image in fullscreenSerbian students and Belgrade residents hold a banner reading ‘We won’t give up the General Staff building’ in Belgrade in November 2025. Photograph: Andrej Isaković/AFP/Getty ImagesA nationalist former propaganda chief under Slobodan Milošević, Vučić hosted the US president’s son Donald Trump Jr and son-in-law Jared Kushner in Belgrade as they developed plans for a $500m hotel and residential tower to add to their global property portfolios.

After the abuse of power charges were brought last December, Kushner’s company announced the project would not proceed “at this time”. Vučić threatened reprisals, calling the prosecutors “corrupt gangs” who “fabricated cases”.

“We have lost an exceptional investment,” the Serbian president said. “I will personally ensure that everyone who participated in causing this damage is held accountable.”

Vučić’s culture minister is among those charged with abuse of power. But a Guardian investigation, drawing on interviews and leaked documents, reveals that the Serbian president himself led the initial meeting where the alleged scheme was discussed. This crucial meeting is not mentioned in the indictment, raising questions about what information the prosecutors are holding back and why.

Representatives of the Trumps and Kushner said they had no part in the removal of the building’s protected status and that it would be “false” to say the Belgrade project was part of a “pay to play” scheme.

Vučić did not respond to requests for comment. His decision to call a snap election means that a hearing at which witnesses might reveal details of his involvement will not take place until after the vote.

2h ago14.26 BSTRussia attempting to destabilise societies across Nato, Romania's Dan says after drone incidentsMeanwhile, Romania’s Nicușor Dan has warned that Russia seeks to “destabilise societies – not just in Romania and Bulgaria, but across European nations, particularly those on the Eastern Flank,” as he responded to overnight drone attacks on ships in Romanian territorial waters of the Black Sea (12:03).

View image in fullscreenRomania’s president Nicușor Dan briefing the media on the margins of the European Council summit in Brussels, Belgium. Photograph: Romanian presidential office YouTube channelBriefing the media in Brussels after his meeting with Nato’s Mark Rutte and Bulgaria’s Rumen Radev (13:01, 14:31), Dan said they discussed the recent incidents in Romania and Bulgaria, and that he believed there was “a need for equipment suited to this new type of challenge.”

He said that’s what happened when Romania was affected by stray drones coming into its territory. “You will recall that … we turned to the allies, some military equipment arrived and the situation stabilised.”

“Clearly, Russia is attempting to destabilise societies – not just in Romania and Bulgaria, but across European nations, particularly those on the Eastern Flank – and to erode support for Ukraine.

Our response is to continue supporting Ukraine, as this is a matter of international law and a matter concerning Romania’s own security.”
